articles.title: Bears DE Montez Sweat suspended for 2 games for violating performance-enhancing drug policy
articles.summary: CHICAGO — The Chicago Bears already faced the prospect of being thin at defensive end for the near future, and now they will be without Montez Sweat for the...
articles.body:
CHICAGO — The Chicago Bears already faced the prospect of being thin at defensive end for the near future, and now they will be without Montez Sweat for the next two games.

The NFL announced Tuesday that Sweat is suspended for two weeks for violating the league's performance-enhancing substances policy. That means he's out for Sunday's Week 6 game in Atlanta and the Week 7 game against the New England Patriots on Thursday, Oct. 22, at Soldier Field.

Defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo left Sunday's 31-7 loss in Green Bay with a quadriceps injury, so his availability is in question.

That means the Bears and defensive coordinator Dennis Allen could be short-handed for multiple games after the defense experienced wildly different performances in the first five games. The Bears surrendered 478 yards and 37 points in the season-opening win at Carolina and were torched by the Packers on Sunday as quarterback Jordan Love had one of the best games of his career, completing 25 of 31 passes for 367 yards and two touchdowns.

Defensive end Austin Booker had two of his four sacks this season in Green Bay and is in line to start now. The Bears have used James Lynch at both tackle and end, and a source said the Bears will restore 2025 second-round pick Shemar Turner to the 53-man roster this week from the physically unable to perform list. Turner has been recovering from a torn ACL suffered last season.

Jamree Kromah, who has yet to play this season, and special teams mainstay Daniel Hardy are also options at end.

Sweat has two sacks, seven tackles and four quarterback hits this season but hasn't been the dominant force the Bears hoped to see.

Coach Ben Johnson repeatedly praised Sweat during the offseason and again in training camp, saying of the 2025 season, "I would argue it was the best year of his career." Sweat had 10 sacks and 18 QB hits last season, and the vibe was that Johnson was attempting to motivate the 30-year-old to reach another level this season.

That hasn't happened to this point, and now the Bears will have to play two games without Sweat while also facing the prospect of Odeyingbo needing some time to heal.

Sweat has one year remaining on his contract with an $18.9 million base salary, a $100,000 workout bonus and a $2 million roster bonus. A decision on his future will be due early in the offseason as the roster bonus is due on the fifth day of the league year. No guaranteed money remains in the contract.

articles.title: Former Bengals quarterback Browning has new team
articles.summary: Former Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Jake Browning reportedly is signing with the Los Angeles Chargers.
articles.body:
Former Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Jake Browning is signing with the Los Angeles Chargers , according to a report via Twitter/X from Tom Pelissero.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers released Browning in late August. In March, the Bucs signed Browning, who became a free agent after the 2025 season.

Browning played in 17 games, making 10 starts, over the past three seasons with the Bengals .

Ja'Marr Chase, Bengals human highlight reel, through the years

The Bengals and Chargers are not scheduled to meet during the 2026 regular season.

Chargers starting QB Justin Herbert has struggled this season, with 937 passing yards, five touchdowns and seven interceptions in the team's first five games, all losses.

Herbert's backup is DJ Uiagalelei. Trey Lance was placed on injured reserve with a groin injury.

In Oct. 2025, Browning acknowledged he was "pissed" about getting benched for Joe Flacco , but added that he would handle the adversity "the right way" as the team started Flacco in Week 6 against Green Bay.

articles.title: Bay Port girls golf finishes strong at WIAA state tournament
articles.summary: The Bay Port girls golf team finished runner-up at the WIAA Division 1 state tournament after a big performance on the final day.
articles.body:
The Bay Port girls golf team entered the WIAA Division 1 state tournament this week with the goal of winning the first championship in program history.

If not for Divine Savior Holy Angels, it would have done it.

The Pirates finished runner-up to the Dashers, finishing with a two-day score of 645 at University Ridge in Madison. DSHA, which won its fourth straight state championship, had a 634.

No team in either D1 or D2 had a better second day than Bay Port, which shot a 309.

It was two strokes better than DSHA and at least seven strokes better than the rest of the 16 squads competing on the big stage.

"I couldn't be more happy with the response after yesterday," Bay Port coach Mitch Meyer said. "Today showed kind of what I have seen all year. They all just kind of put those good rounds together. It happened to only be for one of the two days, but they were really gritty and hit some huge, clutch shots down the stretch that helped us to kind of seal it.

"It was close all the way till the last group was on 18."

Bay Port was making its 10th straight trip to state and had one of its best performances.

The Pirates' top team score came during the alternate spring season in 2021, when they also placed runner-up with a 641.

They had the two best individual scores of any local golfers this time around.

Senior Madelyn Gicius finished tied for seventh overall with a 150, 12 strokes behind state champion McKenna Nelson of Beaver Dam.

Fellow Bay Port senior Myah Johnson was 13th with a 156.

The duo came up big not just in the tournament overall, but on the final hole of their careers to help hold off DeForest and secure the runner-up trophy.

"Going into 18, both of them, we needed their scores," Meyer said. "They knew we needed their scores. Myah ended up hitting a bomb drive and then stuck a shot to five feet and nailed the birdie putt in front of the big crowd on 18.

"As we were walking up, she was talking about how nervous she was to even play 18, it being her last high school hole and everyone watching."

Meyer told Johnson to just go play the hole and they could worry about everything else later.

She responded with a clutch performance.

She has been extremely steady since the day Meyer took over as the coach three years ago. She almost never needs help.

"She had hit kind of an errant drive [on 18], not super in trouble but she was going to have to hit a punch shot," Meyer said. "For the first time in three years, she asked me for advice and ended up hitting a better punch shot than I talked to her about, and then a great chip to like two feet and got up and down for par to seal it for us."

Two other local players placed in the top 20 in D1.

Green Bay Preble co-op senior Emma Cunningham tied for 14th (157), while De Pere senior Emma Hudson was 16th (158).

In D2, Seymour junior Lyla Schueler placed seventh with a 168 to help the Thunder finish fourth in the team standings.

Wrightstown senior Ella Swanson was 12th with a 173, while Seymour junior Maci Heagle was 16th with a 176.

articles.title: Home comfort, renewed confidence: Shubhankar Sharma, Anirban Lahiri target strong week at India Championship at DGC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Shubhankar Sharma arrives at the India Championship with a win behind him at the recently concluded Kapil Dev Invitational in Greater Noida on
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Shubhankar Sharma arrives at the India Championship with a win behind him at the recently concluded Kapil Dev Invitational in Greater Noida on Sunday and a renewed sense of belief. Anirban Lahiri, on the other hand, is hoping that time away from the game will help him return to his best. As the tournament begins at the Delhi Golf Club on Thursday, the two Indians will be looking to make the most of an important week on home soil.The $4 million championship has attracted a strong international field with the likes of Rory Mcllroy, Justin Rose, Aaron Rai and defending champion Tommy Fleetwood to name a few giving the Indian players an opportunity to test themselves against some of the best in the sport.For Sharma, the timing of his victory could prove significant. The two-time winner has endured a frustrating couple of seasons, with the effort he has put into his game not always translating into results.“My main goal of playing last week was to gain some momentum coming into this week. I wasn't thinking about winning,” Sharma said.He wanted to get back into a competitive routine, catch up with familiar faces and work out what needed to change in his game. The victory came as an unexpected bonus, but perhaps its biggest value was the confidence it restored.Sharma has also been making changes to his equipment and technique. After trying different clubs and finding it difficult to maintain consistency in varying conditions on the Tour, he decided to return to equipment he knew well. He has since made a few adjustments and worked on correcting habits that had begun to affect his performances.“The biggest victory was to see that the work that I'm putting in is now showing some result,” he said.What Sharma needs now is to produce his best golf more regularly and carry that form from one tournament to the next. Last week's result has given him reason to believe he is moving in the right direction.“The answer has always been very simple: I want to play with the best,” he said. “It's not about being comfortable for me. It's about being uncomfortable and conquering that feeling and going and performing.”Playing at Delhi Golf Club brings back memories of the early days of his golfing journey. As a young boy, Sharma watched international stars come to India and wondered whether he would ever get the chance to compete in a tournament of that standing at home.He remembers watching Ernie Els at a golf clinic in 2008, when he was around 12 years old. At the time, the prospect of sharing a tournament with leading international players seemed a long way off. Now, he is one of the home players hoping to make his presence felt in front of Indian fans.Sharma also has unfinished business at this championship. Last year, he produced an impressive second round but could not maintain that level over the remainder of the tournament. This time, he wants to build on that performance and avoid the fluctuations that have troubled him in the past.Meanwhile, Lahiri's preparations have been built around a different priority: taking a step back before returning to the demands of professional golf.The 39-year-old spent nearly seven weeks away from competition after a demanding stretch on the circuit. For the first three-and-a-half weeks, he barely touched his clubs, choosing instead to concentrate on his fitness and recovery. The decision followed an assessment with Dr Greg Rose at the Titleist Performance Institute, which helped shape his approach to getting his body back into better condition.Having spent two decades as a professional, Lahiri felt the need to devote more time to his physical well-being rather than continue pushing through a packed schedule.The break also gave him more time at home with his wife and two children, aged four and seven. With professional golf involving frequent travel and long periods away from family, the opportunity to slow down was welcome in its own right.Now back on the course, Lahiri says he feels ready for the challenge ahead.“I'm excited. I'm fresh. Mentally I'm in a really good space,” he said.His experience at Delhi Golf Club could be an advantage, although the course has changed since he last played there. Longer rough and firmer, recontoured greens have altered the test, making accuracy an important part of the equation.Lahiri believes the key will be to keep the ball in play and give himself manageable approaches to the greens. Players who stray from the fairways could find themselves struggling to create birdie chances, while those who strike their irons well should have opportunities to score.With so much quality in the field, Lahiri expects some low scores. But he also knows that players will have to be selective and patient, particularly on a course where one poor shot can undo the work of several good ones.The home setting adds another dimension to the week for both golfers. For Sharma, the tournament offers a chance to reconnect with friends and enjoy the familiarity of playing in India, something that can be difficult to find during a season spent travelling from one international event to another.Lahiri sees the championship as an opportunity to reconnect with the domestic game and help inspire younger golfers. Watching leading professionals compete alongside international stars can give aspiring players a clearer idea of what it takes to reach the highest level.Their routes into the tournament may have been different, but both Indians have reasons to approach the week with optimism.The real test begins on Thursday. A strong field will leave little room for lapses in concentration, and Delhi Golf Club is likely to reward those who combine accuracy with patience over all four rounds.For Sharma, the task is to turn a timely victory into sustained form. articles.title: Chris Mason: Lib Dems rally behind Davey after recent resignations
articles.summary: The BBC's political editor Chris Mason looks at the fallout from the Lib Dem frontbench resignations.
articles.body:
The Liberal Democrats don't tend to go for rhetorical fireworks or verbal kneecappings when grumbling about their leader.

But that doesn't mean there hasn't been grumbling going on. In the last week, two members of Sir Ed Davey's frontbench have resigned because they were unhappy with him, the party's direction and how policy is decided.

It meant the prospect of a lengthy and potentially testy meeting for Sir Ed with his MPs on Tuesday evening.

The Liberal Democrat leader arrived smiling, flanked by several loyal MPs, but made no comment as he entered the room.

Nearly four hours later, when the meeting broke up, his deputy Daisy Cooper said: "There is overwhelming support for Ed in the parliamentary party and a real sense that we need to come together as a group."

Earlier, behind closed doors, we understand Sir Ed told his MPs: "We have made changes. I am happy to embrace more changes. I want us to work as a united front." Another tacit nod to things being less than united recently.

In recent months he has appointed a new chief of staff, Ruth Younger, and James Holt, a veteran of the party's years in coalition government, as political director.

Last week's resignations were described to the BBC by one party figure as a rather Lib Dem insurrection – dissent expressed modestly.

Neither Charlie Maynard, a former Treasury spokesman and Alison Bennett, a former care and carers spokeswoman, have been publicly explicit about the reasons for their departures and both sought to express their concerns to Sir Ed privately and discreetly.

And, it is understood, there was no coordination between them in the timing of their resignations. They were departures that led to fury among some of their colleagues, irritated that it made the party look divided.

The resignations were the most clear indicators yet of an anxiety that has been bubbling away for over a year among some Liberal Democrat MPs. The essence of that anxiety is a fear they are not making enough of an impression and impact for the 72 MPs they have in parliament.

"The big frustration is the lack of cut through, being noticed. We are the biggest third party in the Commons in a century. But parliament doesn't shape things as much as it used to. It's about algorithms now," is how one figure put it.

They added: "In the world of social media there is an incentive, even a financial incentive, to be divisive and extreme. That's a sandpit we refuse to play in."

Nonetheless, the party is planning to up its social media game, but do so in line with what it sees as its authentic temperament and values.

Those around Sir Ed Davey privately acknowledge there is what they claim to be a "small group" of Lib Dem MPs who are not happy with his leadership. It is suggested that number isn't greater than "half a dozen" - a phrase used by several people we have spoken to.

But the anxiety about a perceived lack of impact involves far more MPs than that.

Some previous private critics have been won over by the recent changes to Sir Ed's team and are pleased to see the government talk about issues they care about: the European Union, changing the voting system for Westminster elections and social care in England, for instance.

They also hope the scale of their local campaigning, rather than poor national opinion poll ratings, will be more significant come the next general election.

Al Pinkerton, the party's Europe spokesman, told the BBC there had been a frank exchange of views during the meeting, but Sir Ed's willingness to make changes had been "very well received."

"It is a slog in the middle of a parliament, it's hard being the third party and it's such an enormous leap going from 15 MPs to 72," another party figure present told us. "But we're getting there putting in place the structures to better deal with that and keep MPs happy."

"Why would we get rid of our leader when no one else is pitching to be our leader? We need to let Ed get on with it," said another MP.

But they all know the underlying concern about impact – the challenge of being noticed – is real and not going away.

articles.title: Scottie Scheffler: Will world No 1 break more Tiger Woods records in top spot and who could be next to replace him?
articles.summary: When will someone eventually replace Scottie Scheffler as world No 1? Who is likely to challenge him at the top of the world rankings? And how much longer can he continue his PGA Tour dominance? We take a closer look at Scheffler's Tiger Woods-like spell as the star of men's golf
articles.body:
Scheffler remains the most recent addition to the list of 25 players to have topped the Official World Golf Ranking (OWGR) since its introduction in 1986, with the American having four different spells at No 1 so far in his career.

The latest spell remains unbroken since May 2023, with Scheffler - as of October 12 - entering his 178th consecutive week as world No 1 and with a larger advantage over world No 2 Rory McIlroy than the Northern Irishman has over almost every active professional.

Scheffler is expected to only tee it up once more in 2026, at the Hero World Challenge from December 3-6 - an event he has finished first or second in four times over the last five years - although he already looks to have locked in starting the new year as No 1.

How do the rankings work and why is Scheffler so far ahead?

The world rankings run over a rolling two-year cycle, with points awarded based on the strength of that tournament's field and how high a player finishes on the leaderboard.

A golfer's world ranking then comes from dividing the number of points earned by the number of tournaments someone has played during the cycle, while bonus ranking points are given to players who have won multiple events in a 52-week period.

Scheffler registered two major wins among his six worldwide titles in 2025 and already has three victories in 2026, a campaign in which his remarkable consistency has seen him post top-three finishes in half of his 20 worldwide starts.

"He's the best player in the world by a country mile," said Sky Sports' Andrew Coltart. "It's his distance control and his ability to get scoring irons pin-high basically all the time, along with an incredible level of consistency.

"Also, very importantly, I think it's his golfing IQ and his understanding of how his game is and where his game is at - that's why he's the dominant force in the game."

How has Scheffler cemented himself as No 1?

Claiming his first three PGA Tour titles in a seven-week stretch saw Scheffler take top spot for the first time in March 2022, a fortnight before his maiden major victory at The Masters, a position he held until McIlroy overtook him that October.

Scheffler enjoyed a one-week burst back at the top after his 2023 WM Phoenix Open win and another four-week run after winning The Players the following month, before Jon Rahm leapfrogged him with his second major win secured at Augusta National.

Rahm would lose top spot when Scheffler tied-second at the PGA Championship a month later, with no player since able to end his ever-increasing reign as world No 1.

"He has managed to stay at the top for so long because he has no weaknesses across his game," Sky Sports' Nick Dougherty said. "He was once a below-average putter, but he's now world class and a top-10 putter.

"The iron play is peerless - he's not just the best, he's the best by a mile when he's at his very peak. He leads birdie average and leads bogey avoidance. When you look at all of that together, there's just a reason he's better than everyone in every area."

Only Woods and Greg Norman have spent longer in their careers at world No 1 than Scheffler, who aged just 30 has already won 22 PGA Tour titles - including four majors and three legs of the career Grand Slam - and cemented his status among the greats.

Woods was world No 1 for 281 consecutive weeks from June 2005 to October 2010, breaking his own record of 264 weeks previously held from August 1999 to September 2004, with Scheffler the closest to ever seriously threaten those historic runs.

Scheffler would need to remain in top spot until October 2035 to overtake Woods' career total of 683 weeks as No 1 but only until mid-October 2028 to break the longest consecutive spell, although he has plenty of work to do to reach that milestone.

"I have absolutely no valid reason why he won't [pass 281 weeks], when you look at what he's doing right now, but the level rises around you," Dougherty added. "Whether it's Rory coming back for him again or whether he has a little bit of a slump.

"Golf is just really hard to be that good for that long. Other than Tiger Woods we've never really seen it, other than Scheffler. There's new kids on the block too and they're all hungry, so I've got a feeling someone will get to him before then."

Dame Laura Davies added: "No [he won't break the record], because of the challenging pack behind him. It won't be that he necessarily drops off that much, I just think there's way too many good players just in behind him. Over two years, it's a long time."

Will Woods or McIlroy ever return to world No 1?

Woods is currently listed as 'unranked' in the OWGR standings, having not played an official event since The Open in July 2024 and only completed four 72-hole tournaments over the last six seasons.

The 50-year-old has previously ruled out a return to full-time professional golf and is unlikely to ever return to being one of the world's best, but McIlroy has continued to be Scheffler's closest challenger to the No 1 spot.

McIlroy has been no lower than third in the world rankings since Scheffler became No 1 and has been second since last March, with the Northern Irishman winning back-to-back Masters titles over the last two seasons.

"I think McIlroy still has another stint there [at No 1] because, when he's at his absolute strength, he is definitely alongside Scheffler," Dougherty insisted. "I think he can take him on his day, he just isn't as consistent as Scottie."

Coltart added: "For McIlroy to get back to world No 1 is really tough. He's at a different stage of his life and he's attained, arguably, what he ever set out in his life to attain.

"He's older, he's got different aspirations. I don't think the fire is necessarily there that it was in his belly when he was in his early 20s. It will be very difficult for Rory to do that and I hope that he proves me wrong."

Who is likely to be Scheffler's replacement?

Matt Fitzpatrick has moved to world No 3 after winning four times in 2026, although the Zurich Classic of New Orleans did not offer world ranking points, while Players champion Cameron Young and US Open winner Wyndham Clark complete the top five.

Scheffler previously jumped from world No 15 to world No 1 in a six-week burst in 2022, highlighting that rapid rises are possible, although any of his challengers would likely require multiple more victories to be next in line for the world No 1 spot.

"If it's not Rory to go past him, it's hard to imagine who it would be among this current crop," Dougherty admitted. "It could be someone like Jackson Koivun, who is a new arrival and he's a superstar that clearly stands out already.

"It could be one of these young guns, it could even be someone we don't know yet, that's going to displace him at the top of the game."

Chris Gotterup, Sam Burns and Si Woo Kim have also made big rises up the world rankings in 2026, while Koivun and Miles Russell are others tipped to have big futures on the PGA Tour.

"There's half a dozen of them that could string together results, because that's what world No 1 is all about - consistency," Davies said. "At some point, someone will go past him. Who will that be? We'll have to wait and see.

"Watch this space, because they're all very good. He [Scheffler] is just that little bit better at the moment."

articles.title: Packers fans will love MarShawn Lloyd’s hate for the Bears after 2 TD performance
articles.summary: The Green Bay Packers and the Chicago Bears added another chapter to their storied rivalry after facing off at Lambeau Field on Sunday. The Packers made minc...
articles.body:
The Green Bay Packers and the Chicago Bears added another chapter to their storied rivalry after facing off at Lambeau Field on Sunday. The Packers made mincemeat of the Bears , 31-7, with MarShawn Lloyd, Jordan Love, and Christian Watson starring in the blowout win.

Lloyd had 10 carries for 31 yards and two touchdowns, Love went 25-of-31 for 367 yards, two touchdowns, and zero interceptions, and Watson added six receptions for 143 yards and two touchdowns.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Following his impressive performance, the 25-year-old Lloyd made a lovely comment about the Bears on "The Schultz Report."

"Hate them. Hate them with a passion. But that comes with it. Rivalry is everything. You go through it in college. It's cool to come out on top," said the third-year running back.

The Packers lead the all-time head-to-head against the Bears , 110-98-6.

When the former USC standout was asked which he abhors more—Green Bay or Notre Dame—Lloyd had to think for a bit before coming up with an answer.

"The same. Definitely the same. Yeah, for sure. I don't like either one of them," said Lloyd.

He is looking to stay healthy after a string of injuries hampered his first two years with the Packers. Before this season, he had only appeared in one game.

If his explosive showing against the Bears was any indication, Lloyd should only improve Green Bay's ground attack, which has been an issue.

The Packers will try to notch their third straight win on Sunday against another arch-nemesis, the Dallas Cowboys.

articles.title: McIlroy defiende la mano dura del DP World Tour con el LIV
articles.standfirst: El golfista noirlandés pide a sus compañeros que elijan en qué circuito desean jugar
articles.summary: El golfista noirlandés pide a sus compañeros que elijan en qué circuito desean jugar
articles.body: El golfista noirlandés Rory McIlroy, número dos del mundo, mostró su respaldo este miércoles a la nueva regla establecida por el DP World Tour de que aquellos jugadores que se inscriban en el nuevo proyecto LIV 2.0 no podrán ser miembros del circuito europeo, al defender que es necesario cumplir las normas. "Si te inscribes en LIV 2.0, no serás miembro del DP World Tour. Así de simple", subrayó McIlroy en una rueda de prensa en Nueva Delhi, donde este jueves comienza el torneo de la India, integrado en el circuito europeo. El DP World Tour permitía a esta temporada compaginar la participación en sus torneos de los jugadores de LIV con algunas condiciones, pero a partir de 2027, ha determinado que no será posible la doble membresía. "El DP World Tour ha tomado una buena decisión, porque el panorama del gol ha estado cambiando constantemente durante los últimos cuatro o cinco años. Ha llegado el punto en que los jugadores tendrán que decidir qué es importante para ellos y qué es lo que realmente quieren hacer", argumentó el doble campeón del Masters de Augusta. A su juicio, el circuito europeo ha sido "muy comprensivo" con los jugadores de LIV y ahora "está en todo su derecho de cambiar las reglas" en un momento "de tanta incertidumbre" que atraviesa la liga que Arabia Saudí creó en 2022 y que dejó de financiar el pasado mes de agosto. "Esta es la manera de proteger su negocio y fortalecer el circuito al máximo (...) Tiene derecho a modificar y adaptar las reglas cuando lo consideren necesario para proteger sus intereses o derechos", justificó el golfista norirlandés. Tras la retirada del fondo soberano saudí, LIV se ha declarado en bancarrota con la pretensión de poner en marcha el proyecto 2.0 con otros inversores. Algunos jugadores que han militado en la liga saudí, como los españoles Jon Rahm y David Puig, ya han confirmado que no seguirán en la nueva versión del circuito.

articles.summary: LPGA commissioner Craig Kessler says Good Good Golf deserves forgiveness after the controversial Callaway ad that rocked the entire golf world.
articles.body: LPGA commissioner Craig Kessler believes in something that has largely been lost, not only in sports, but across society as a whole: forgiveness. During the "Tuned In" summit hosted by Front Office Sports on Tuesday, Kessler was asked to share his take on the controversial Good Good Golf advertisement with Callaway that took over the golf world and social media back in August. Kessler's opinion on the ad — which featured Good Good co-founder Garrett Clark pushing member Alexis Miestowski to the ground — was one based in common sense. Like most, he couldn't believe the advertisement was greenlit to begin with, but he isn't on board with the idea of cancelling the brand over an admittedly huge mistake. articles.title: LIV Golf CEO said to have slipped up when speaking about the tour’s Saudi Funding
articles.summary: LIV Golf looks to be on its last legs. The tour is bankrupt without its Saudi funding; players are leaving in droves, and it’s unclear how the tour will surv...
articles.body:
The tour is bankrupt without its Saudi funding; players are leaving in droves, and it's unclear how the tour will survive next season or beyond. The DP World Tour dealt LIV its latest blow, declaring that LIV players will not be eligible for membership.

For years, LIV golfers have said they joined the tour because they're passionate about growing the game worldwide. Many insisted it had nothing to do with the eye-watering sums of money the Saudi Public Investment Fund was throwing at them.

But what LIV CEO Scott O'Neil said recently has exposed those comments for being total nonsense.

LIV Golf CEO lets slip on Saudi Public Investment Fund

The moment LIV Golf went bankrupt and the ridiculous amounts of money stopped being thrown at players, the talk about growing the game suddenly fell silent. Players have been leaving the tour in droves in recent weeks, and even CEO Scott O'Neil has reflected on how the tour used to do business.

Speaking at a Sportico Conference in London, O'Neil said, "Saudi-type business plan to, as I like to say, a business business plan."

And with these comments, analyst Trey Wingo says O'Neil put the entire "grow the game" narrative to bed.

Speaking on Trey Wingo Golf, "It bothers me immensely that of the LIV legacy, it's going to be generational players got more money and businesses, and independent contractors got shafted. That is something that's going to bother me immensely.

"The 30 for 30 on LIV is going to be fantastic in all the good and possibly bad ways it could be. Here's what I would say about that. Yes, but they never would have gotten the players to go if they didn't give them obscene amounts of money.

"And that's the problem. It was never about growing the game. That was a ruse. It was a con. You know, it was sleight of hand. It was it was look over at my left hand when my right hand is over here. The whole thing was never about building a sustainable business model.

"Scott O'Neil said that at the Sportico Conference in London. 'We went from a Saudi business model to actually having an actual business model.' I mean, that's it in a nutshell. It was never a business model to begin with. It was an attempt to be a disruptive force in one of the greatest sports in the world so they could have a seat at the table. That's all it ever was supposed to be.

"And some credit I'll give Graham McDowell and the others who finally acknowledge that when they're like, 'Yeah, I never wish I'd spouted this grow the game stuff. I just went for the obscene checks.'"

It's true that some players, like McDowell, have backtracked on their LIV Golf stance, but many have tried to sneak off silently into the night. At least we can all now recognize that it was only ever about the money.

articles.title: Burnham rules out coalition with Greens after 'Zionism is racism' motion
articles.summary: Andy Burnham condemns the motion approved by Green Party members and says his party would "have nothing to do with it".
articles.body:
Andy Burnham has said he will not support his party forming a partnership with the Green Party as long as it maintains a policy of defining Zionism as a form of racism.

Speaking in the House of Commons, the prime minister said the motion, backed by Green members at its party conference earlier this month, was "wrong" and "antisemitic" and Labour would have "nothing to do with it".

The motion said Zionism was an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/ or domination of the non-Jewish population".

It was criticised by Jewish groups, as well as four Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".

Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" and that he had wanted to see it amended.

However, he has defended the substantial part of the motion arguing that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by racist ideology" was "obvious". Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.

The motion, having been backed by members, has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

The subject was raised during Prime Minister's Questions, when Conservative MP Dame Harriett Baldwin urged Burnham to "rule out co-operating" with the Green Party.

Burnham replied: "Can I condemn the motion that was passed unequivocally.

"It is wrong, it is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it.

"We will always take the right response when it comes to any partnerships we have with other parties.

"We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds the position that has recently been adopted."

Labour is currently in coalition with the Green Party on some local councils including Sheffield.

A Downing Street spokesman would not confirm if the prime minister's position extended to local areas or just applied to national government level.

The adoption of the motion has prompted some Green Party figures to call for changes to the party's rules.

Last week, MP Ellie Chowns told the BBC: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813 - a small fraction of the 230,000 members in the party.

Key backer of the motion Lubna Speitan has defended the motion arguing that it aimed to oppose "racist systems of oppression" adding: "We stand united against all forms of racism and discrimination - no exemptions."
